profile.reading: This registry row, named Involta-Akron and covering the operator's Akron I and Akron II buildings, sits at 191 East Miller Avenue, Akron, Ohio 44301, in Summit County. The operator's public site, still resolving at the involta.com domain but branded Ark Data Centers throughout, including in its own copyright footer, confirms this is a genuine company rebrand rather than a sale to an unrelated third party. This registry records the current name as Ark Data Centers with Involta retained as former operator per its standard no-deletion policy. Ark's own Ohio operations page describes this Akron location as providing 5 megawatts of power capacity and 20,000 square feet of conditioned data center space, with 2N UPS battery backup and N+1 computer room air conditioning, and states the Akron and Cleveland area facilities are linked by a dedicated fiber ring offering millisecond latency between sites. Ark's own about page states the company was founded in 2007 as a Tier III edge data center provider and now operates purpose built, owned and operated facilities across eight markets including Arizona, Idaho, Iowa, Minnesota, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. Company wide certifications listed on Ark's own site include HITRUST CSF, PCI, NIST, HIPAA, ITAR, and ITIL. A facility specific aggregator listing independently names Ark Data Centers Akron 1, Akron 2, and an Akron Campus entry all sharing this same 191 East Miller Avenue address, referencing Involta only in historical description, corroborating both the rebrand and the address applied here. No specific year this building opened was located this session. Summit County, Ohio, home to Akron, sits within the broader Northeast Ohio market that also includes Cleveland and Independence, a region with a long industrial and manufacturing base that has more recently attracted edge and enterprise colocation providers like Ark seeking proximity to Midwest healthcare, manufacturing, and logistics customers rather than the hyperscale cloud tenants concentrated in larger markets like Northern Virginia or Chicago.

reading.body:
Involta-Akron, operating as Ark Data Centers across two buildings in Akron, Ohio, publishes 5 megawatts of IT capacity. At 250 watts per rack, a conservative density for general colocation, this translates to roughly 20,000 racks; at 40 kilowatts per rack, a typical AI training density, the same power supports approximately 125 racks of accelerator infrastructure. The facility occupies 20,000 square feet of conditioned space, certified to Tier III design and claiming 100 percent power delivery availability. Ark Data Centers was founded in 2007 as a Tier III edge provider and now operates across eight regional markets including Ohio, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and Arizona; this Akron location is linked by dedicated fiber to the operator's Cleveland facility.

The Akron campus sits in Northeast Ohio, a market built around manufacturing, healthcare, and logistics rather than hyperscale cloud. Ohio has 76 mapped data center facilities, but only 8 publish power capacity figures. Involta-Akron ranks ninth among those eight published sites, representing 8 percent of Ohio's disclosed total of 60.4 megawatts. The state context is not published, but the operator's own site states the Akron and Cleveland area facilities are connected by millisecond-latency fiber, suggesting a regional cluster strategy rather than standalone facility placement.

For AI workloads, Involta-Akron's 5 megawatts is modest absolute capacity suitable for inference, smaller training jobs, or edge model serving, not large-scale foundation model training. The facility's Tier III certification qualifies it for enterprise and colocation tenants requiring reliability over raw scale. Whether Ark Data Centers' current tenant base includes AI workloads is not published.
